title: Trump Administration Plans to Revoke Up to 200,000 Temporary Visas in Asylum Crackdown
excerpt: The State Department is targeting B-1 and B-2 visa holders who entered as temporary visitors and then applied for asylum, in what could be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history.
body:
• The State Department is coordinating with DHS to revoke B-1 and B-2 visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who entered the U.S. as temporary visitors and then applied for asylum
  • If carried out at full scale, it would be the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history, covering visas issued between 2016 and 2026
  • Immigration attorneys say the revocations are largely symbolic and would not directly result in deportations, since overstayed visas are already invalid
  • The administration has already revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump took office, targeting various categories of foreign nationals

The Trump administration is preparing to revoke up to 200,000 temporary business and tourism visas in what officials describe as a crackdown on foreigners who entered the United States as short-term visitors and then filed for asylum to remain permanently — a move that, if executed at full scale, would constitute the largest mass visa revocation in American history.

The State Department is working with the Department of Homeland Security to identify holders of B-1 business and B-2 tourism visas issued between 2016 and 2026 who subsequently applied for or are currently seeking asylum, according to State Department documents and U.S. officials cited by the Associated Press.

'A Privilege, Not a Right'

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio's leadership, we are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right. Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation."

https://x.com/essenviews/status/2092791010967306346 — Tommy Pigott, State Department Spokesperson

The State Department has framed the effort as targeting fraud — cases where individuals allegedly obtained temporary visas while secretly planning to seek permanent residence through asylum. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau reinforced the message on X, alleging that the American immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims."

The department has not explained how investigators will distinguish between individuals who entered with the intent to file asylum claims and those who decided to seek protection after arriving because conditions in their home countries changed. The revocations will occur on a rolling basis rather than all at once, with the department saying the final number "remains dynamic."

Legal Impact May Be Limited

Despite the dramatic scale of the announcement, immigration experts say the practical consequences may be far more modest than the headline numbers suggest.

Immigration attorney Nicolette Glazer called the plan an "empty effort" with limited legal consequences. If an immigrant has already overstayed their temporary visa, that visa is already invalid — revoking it does not create any new grounds for deportation or change their legal status in a meaningful way, she told NPR.

"It's pretty obvious at this point that the administration went through immigration laws and regulations with a fine-tooth comb, and they're just doing everything that they have the authority to do," said Camille Mackler, an immigration policy consultant. "I think it's mostly the message that it sends."

A source familiar with the matter confirmed to CNN that the revocations would not result in immediate deportations. Most asylum seekers with pending cases would simply be re-categorized but would retain their ability to pursue their claims through the immigration court system.

Implications for Indian Visa Holders

While the State Department has not singled out any nationality, the review covers a decade of visa issuance during which Indian nationals were consistently among the top recipients of B-1 and B-2 visas. Indians account for a significant share of both business and tourism visa holders, and a subset have historically pursued adjustment of status through various legal channels after arriving in the U.S.

The announcement adds to a growing list of immigration enforcement actions under the Trump administration that directly affect the Indian diaspora, including the proposed $103,000 H-1B fee, executive orders targeting birthright citizenship, and restrictions on F-1 student visa duration.

Part of a Broader Campaign

The planned revocations build on more than 175,000 visas the State Department says it has already revoked under the current administration, targeting foreign nationals the department said committed crimes, violated visa terms, or posed a security risk. The administration has also revoked visas from international students and immigrants who made political comments online.

Glazer noted that the effort could still affect people who have been in the United States for years and have established roots, including those with U.S. citizen children. For asylum seekers with legitimate claims of persecution, the revocation of their original entry visa adds another layer of uncertainty to an already precarious legal situation.

The rolling nature of the revocations means the full scope and impact will unfold over the coming months, with the administration retaining discretion over which cases to prioritize and how aggressively to pursue enforcement against those whose visas are cancelled.
